lines.text: Now turn to Section Four. You will hear part of a lecture on peat bogs and carbon storage.
Questions thirty-one to thirty-four. Complete the summary. Write no more than two words and/or a number for each answer. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-four.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-four.
This lecture examines how peat bogs store carbon that would otherwise enter the air.
Wet peat is often called a carbon sponge — a slow, waterlogged layer that locks plant remains away from oxygen.
The key plant in that layer is sphagnum, a moss that holds water and keeps the bog acidic.
In Britain, peat covers about four percent of the land surface — four, not a third of the map.
Those same bogs, however, hold about thirty percent of the country's soil carbon — a large share in a small area.
Questions thirty-five and thirty-six. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. The options are on your question paper only. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-five and thirty-six.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-five and thirty-six.
When we interview hill farmers, the complaint they raise most often is not paperwork and not peat prices — it is lost grazing after fences go up around wet restoration sites.
lines.note: Paper: A lost grazing; B extra paperwork; C low peat prices.

lines.text: As for restoration, planting trees on dry peat has mixed results, and boardwalks mainly help visitors. The approach with the strongest field evidence so far is raising the water table — rewetting — so sphagnum can return. Rewetting is a method, not a map-area statistic.
lines.note: Paper: A tree planting on dry peat; B visitor boardwalks; C raising the water table. Land cover stays 4%; soil carbon share stays 30%.

lines.text: Questions thirty-seven to forty. Complete the notes. Write no more than two words and/or a number for each answer. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-seven to forty.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-seven to forty.
Our case study is Raven Fen, which monitored ditches over six years.

Among plots that had stayed dry for more than twenty years, specialist bog plants were about twenty-five percent less common than on wet control plots of similar size — twenty-five percent lower cover, not twenty-five percent of all British peat.
The site now issues dipwells for water-level checks, because guesswork from the path was missing summer drops.
Managers are also blocking deep drains rather than mowing in July, because deep drains dry the sponge every season and that is worse than a single summer cut.
Next week we will look at saltmarsh carbon. Thank you.
That is the end of the Listening test.
